archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (possession-first)
archetype.definition: A team that controls 5-on-5 play as well as anyone in the league but sits at .500 because its goalies and finishers are near the bottom of the league, so its process is well ahead of its results.

report.headline: The league's best shot share, buried by bottom-five goaltending and finishing
report.take:
Eight games in, New Jersey's 4-4-0 record and 13th-place site rank undersell what is happening on the ice. The Devils lead the league in both 5-on-5 shares, with a .609 xGF % and a .62 CF %, and put 35 shots on goal a game, also first, against a league average of 27.2. They allow 24.9, 10th fewest. By territory and chance quality this is a top team. By the scoreboard it is a slightly negative one, at -0.25 Goal Diff / GP.

The gap between those two pictures comes from the two percentages a team controls least over short samples. The skaters are shooting .089 in all situations, 28th, against a league .113. The goalies are stopping .869, 27th, against a league .893, and Goalies GSAx sits at -4.7, 29th. Together that is an all-situations PDO of 95.9, 30th in the league. The roster grades show where the problem sits: forwards B+, blueline B+, goaltending D-. Jake Allen (.876, -2.9 GSAx) and Nico Daws (.857, -2.7) have both been below average, so this is not one bad goalie dragging down a good one.

The numbers also hide some real problems. The penalty kill is at .696, 27th, and opposing defensemen are feasting. The Devils have allowed 3.13 points a game to blueliners, worst in the league against expectation. Defensemen take a .329 share of the points scored against New Jersey, compared with .242 league-wide. That pattern fits point shots beating weak goaltending and a leaky kill rather than a 5-on-5 structure problem, which the shot shares say is fine. Goaltending has been a recurring weakness here before: GSAx was -11.4 in 2023-24 and -3.5 last season, while the one recent year it was strong (+23.3 in 2024-25) the Devils had a top-five defense.

The direction is encouraging. Over the last five games they are 3-2-0 and have outscored opponents 19-14, including a 7-1 win over the Rangers. Jack Hughes (9 points, .646 xGF %), Jesper Bratt (.693 xGF %) and Luke Hughes (7th of 242 defensemen, 24 minutes a night) are driving play. The current pace of 82 standings points is the floor if the percentages stay this low. A team that out-chances opponents this badly usually climbs once its save % moves back toward league average.

strengths.title: League-best 5-on-5 control
strengths.body: New Jersey owns the puck and the chances: first in xGF % and CF %, and first in shots on goal by a wide margin. That edge shows up across the lineup, from Bratt and the Hughes brothers down to depth forwards, rather than coming from one line. Shot share stabilizes faster than any percentage stat, so this is the part of the start most likely to hold.

strengths.title: Top-end talent driving play
strengths.body: Jack Hughes leads the team with 9 points and a .646 xGF % in 21 minutes a night. Bratt ranks 13th among left wings, and Luke Hughes is 7th of 242 defensemen. Both skater groups grade B+. A team with this much quality at the top can keep driving play while it waits for its finishing and goaltending to recover.

strengths.title: Recent results catching up
strengths.body: The last five games went 3-2-0 with a +5 differential, after a 1-2 start that included a 0-6 loss on Long Island. The scoreboard is starting to reflect the territorial edge, though five games is still a small window.

concerns.title: Goaltending is giving games away
concerns.body: A .869 team save % and -4.7 GSAx rank near the bottom of the league, and both goalies are below expected. Some of that is eight-game noise, but recent history shows the Devils can run a negative GSAx across a full season, as they did in 2023-24 and 2025-26. This is the single biggest risk to the rebound case.

concerns.title: Penalty kill and point shots
concerns.body: The PK is killing only .696, 27th and far below the league's .790. Opposing defensemen are scoring at the worst rate in the league relative to expectation. Weak goaltending explains part of both numbers, but the kill was around .80 or better in each of the previous four seasons, so a structural slip is possible too.

concerns.title: Cold finishing on high volume
concerns.body: An .089 shooting % ranks 28th even though the Devils lead the league in shots. A lot of volume from the point could hold the rate down somewhat, but numbers this low on this many quality chances tend to rise.

trend.note: A volatile 1-2 start, including a 0-6 loss, has given way to a 3-2-0 stretch with a +5 differential over the last five. The shot shares have been strong throughout.

weekAhead.headline: Three home games, including struggling LA, before a road test at Dallas
weekAhead.body:
Three of the four games are in Newark, and the middle of the week is soft. Anaheim sits 19th and is getting out-chanced (.478 xGF %, 24.1 shots a game). Los Angeles is 0-4-2 and ranked 31st, with F grades in goal and on the blueline and a .861 save %. For a team leading the league in shot volume, the Kings are a good chance for the shooting percentage to recover.

The bookends are harder. Colorado (8th) is scoring well, but much of that rests on a .146 shooting % and a 106.8 PDO, so the Avalanche are running hot the way the Devils are running cold. Dallas has the league's best defense on paper, but it comes from a .944 save % and +9.6 GSAx, not shot suppression. The Stars' .487 xGF % suggests New Jersey should control that game territorially. Winning it will come down to beating a hot goalie.

keyMatchups.title: Devils PK vs Anaheim's power play
keyMatchups.body: Anaheim converts at .269, 6th in the league, and New Jersey's kill is 27th. If the Ducks win the special-teams battle, it can cancel out a 5-on-5 edge the Devils should hold easily.

keyMatchups.title: Shot volume vs LA's goaltending
keyMatchups.body: The Kings' goalies stop .861 and their PK kills only .619, both near the bottom of the league. Against a team averaging 35 shots, this is the likeliest game of the week for New Jersey's finishing to come back.

keyMatchups.title: Dallas's hot goaltending
keyMatchups.body: Dallas allows the fewest points to opposing forwards relative to expectation and stops .944, both league-best figures driven by goaltending. Its 5-on-5 shares are below average, so the Devils should get plenty of looks. The test is whether they can beat a goalie playing this well.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the Devils' save % climbs toward league average. If it does, the shot dominance turns into wins.

restOfSeason.body:
The 5-on-5 dominance is the sustainable part. This roster is controlling play better than the 2022-23 team did, and that team posted 112 points on a .560 xGF %. The 95.9 all-situations PDO is the part that should regress upward. Shooting near .089 is unlikely to last for a team generating this much, and a .869 save % is well below even a mediocre tandem's usual level. If the goalies merely reach average, the Devils should move into the Metropolitan playoff picture comfortably.

The caveat is that the goaltending weakness is not new. Neither Allen nor Daws has shown above-average form, and the penalty kill has a real problem to fix. Our projection sits between the two cases: a clear improvement on the current 82-point pace, but short of contender territory unless the save % fully recovers.
swingFactors: Allen and Daws reaching league-average save %

confidence.note: Eight games is thin, but shot shares this strong are among the most reliable early signals.
